title: The Miracles of the Qur'an
author: Original guide — the Qur'an's challenge, the Sunnah and the sources
source: Coran, hadiths authentifiés, travaux classiques de l'i'jâz et sources scientifiques et historiques publiées (voir chapitre Sources)

chapters.title: Le défi lancé par le Coran
chapters.text:
## A book that stakes its own authenticity

There is a very simple way to refute the Qur'an, and the Qur'an itself points it out. It would be enough to produce a comparable text.

This is what is called the *tahaddi*, the challenge. It runs through the revelation, and what is striking is that it **narrows** — as though the demand were lowered as the incapacity was confirmed.

**First, the whole book:**

*"Say: 'If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like of it, even if they were to each other assistants.'"* (Qur'an 17:88)

**Then ten suras:**

*"Or do they say, 'He invented it'? Say: 'Then bring ten suras like it, invented, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.'"* (Qur'an 11:13)

**Then a single sura:**

*"And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our Servant, then produce a sura the like thereof and call upon your witnesses besides Allah, if you are truthful. But if you do not — and you will never be able to — then fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones."* (Qur'an 2:23-24)

A single sura. The shortest in the Qur'an, *al-Kawthar*, has three verses and about ten words.

## Why that challenge carried weight

Addressed to any other people, this challenge might have passed unnoticed. Addressed to the Arabs of the seventh century, it targeted precisely the field in which they excelled.

Poetry was their sovereign art. The tribes held contests at Ukaz, the best poems — the *Mu'allaqat* — were hung up, and a poet could make or break the standing of a clan. Mastery of the language was social capital as much as talent.

It is these men whom the Qur'an challenges. And these same men, who had every interest in meeting it — a rebuttal would have cost less than a war — chose exile, boycott, and then arms.

## What the challenge actually targets

The point deserves stating clearly, because it is often misunderstood. The challenge is not about the quantity of information, nor about scientific advance, nor about beauty in a decorative sense. It is about the **nature of the discourse itself**: its composition, its bearing, its way of saying.

That is why the classical scholars concentrated their work on language — we come to it in the next chapter. And that is also why this book starts there: not with recent discoveries, but with the ground the Qur'an chooses for itself.

## A distinction useful for what follows

Muslim tradition distinguishes two words that English renders poorly:

- The ***mu'jiza*** is the sign granted to a prophet to authenticate his mission. Every prophet received one, suited to his age: Moses' staff before the magicians, the healing of the sick for Jesus before the physicians.
- The ***aya*** is the sign in the broad sense — a verse, but also a phenomenon of creation that invites reflection. The word is the same, and that is no accident.

The miracle of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has a particularity: it is **the book itself**. Other miracles end with the one who performs them; this one remains open and verifiable fourteen centuries later.

*"And is it not sufficient for them that We revealed to you the Book which is recited to them?"* (Qur'an 29:51)

## What this book covers

Five areas, from the most solid to the most debated — and that is deliberate:

1. **The miracle of the speech** — the composition, the man who transmitted it, the coherence across twenty-three years, the preservation of the text.
2. **The prophecies fulfilled** — what the Qur'an announced and history confirmed.
3. **The signs in creation** — the verses that describe the world, and how to read them without forcing them.
4. **The signs granted to the Prophet ﷺ** — what the Sunnah reports.
5. **The sources** — every reference, verifiable.

chapters.title: L'inimitabilité de la parole
chapters.text:
## The heart of the matter

For more than a thousand years, when Muslim scholars set out to explain how the Qur'an is inimitable, they did not talk about astronomy or embryology. They talked about **language**.

This is the discipline of *i'jaz al-bayani* — the inimitability of the expression. It has produced a considerable literature, and two works are authoritative in it.

## Al-Baqillani: the text belongs to no genre

Abu Bakr al-Baqillani (d. 403 AH / 1013) wrote *I'jaz al-Qur'an*, in which he advances an argument from form.

The Arabic language had clearly established genres: poetry with its metres, the rhymed prose of the soothsayers (*saj'*), the speech of orators. Each had its rules, its effects, its limits.

The Qur'an fits none of them. It is not poetry — it has neither metre nor regular rhyme. It is not *saj'* — it sometimes has the cadence, never the mechanism. It is not ordinary prose — its density and rhythm set it apart.

Al-Baqillani draws his argument from this: a human author works **within** a genre. To produce a text belonging to none, while surpassing each on its own ground, and to sustain it across an entire book — that is what no pen has repeated.

## Al-Jurjani: the theory of *nazm*

'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani (d. 471 AH / 1078) goes further, and his contribution remains the summit of classical Arabic literary theory. His two works — *Asrar al-balagha* (The Secrets of Rhetoric) and *Dala'il al-i'jaz* (The Proofs of Inimitability) — take on a received idea.

It was readily said that the beauty of the Qur'an lay in its words, chosen one by one. Al-Jurjani shows this is false: taken in isolation, the words of the Qur'an are everyone's words. The miracle is not in the lexicon.

It is in the ***nazm*** — the arrangement. The way the words are ordered, the way the syntax is chosen from among the possibilities, the way each element is placed exactly where it yields its full effect of meaning.

His demonstration is technical and can be checked: in Arabic, word order is flexible, and each shift alters the emphasis carried by one element or another. Al-Jurjani shows, verse after verse, that the construction chosen is never indifferent — that another order, grammatically correct, would always weaken something.

It is a strong thesis: **meaning and form are not separable**. You cannot say the same thing differently without saying something else.

## An example: the law of retaliation

*"And there is for you in legal retribution a life, O people of understanding, that you may become righteous."* (Qur'an 2:179)

The Arabs had a celebrated formula for this idea: *"killing is what curbs killing"*. It passed for a model of concision.

The rhetoricians compared the two and noted several things. The Qur'anic phrase is shorter. It avoids repeating the word "killing". It sets two opposites against one another — retribution and **life** — where the adage sets nothing against anything, which makes the idea graspable at once: the sanction is not there to deal death, but to preserve life. And it adds a purpose the adage ignores: *"that you may become righteous"*.

A formula held to be unsurpassable is found surpassed on its own ground.

## What is particular about this argument

It has a strength and a weakness that must both be named honestly.

Its strength: it bears on what the Qur'an itself puts at stake, it depends on no future discovery, and it has not shifted in fourteen centuries. It is the most stable ground there is.

Its limit: it **presupposes Arabic**. A translation, however careful, does not carry the *nazm* across — it carries the meaning. That is why Muslims call translations "translations of the meaning" and not "the Qur'an".

This does not shut out the non-Arabic-speaking reader: the other chapters of this book are fully accessible. But it is honest to say that the central argument is played out in one language, and that one cannot fully judge it without that language.

## The effect on its first hearers

An episode reported by the early biographers says what the treatises demonstrate.

Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, one of the chiefs of Quraysh and a fine judge of poetry, listens to the Prophet ﷺ recite. His peers ask him to name what he has heard, so they can discredit it. He answers, in substance: this is neither poetry, nor magic, nor the speech of a soothsayer; it has a sweetness and a beauty of its own, its root is fertile and its branch bears fruit.

Then, under pressure from his own people, he falls back on the accusation of magic — for want of anything better. The sura *al-Muddaththir* (74:18-25) evokes that inner deliberation: a man who reflects, weighs, and ends by saying the opposite of what he saw.

That scene sums up the matter: the difficulty was not in denying the text, it was in **classifying** it.

chapters.title: Un messager qui ne lisait pas
chapters.text:
## A man who could neither read nor write

The Qur'an describes the Prophet ﷺ as *ummi* — one who neither reads nor writes:

*"Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet (ummi), whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel…"* (Qur'an 7:157)

And it draws an argument from this explicitly:

*"And you did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you inscribe one with your right hand. Otherwise the falsifiers would have had cause to doubt."* (Qur'an 29:48)

The reasoning is direct: had he been a man of letters, familiar with the ancient scriptures, the charge of compilation would have had purchase. It had none — the earliest opponents, who had known him since childhood, never accused him of having read.

## What they reproached him with, and what they could not

The objections of Quraysh are preserved in the Qur'an itself, which cites them in order to answer them. They are instructive for what they contain — and for what is missing.

He was accused of being a poet (36:69), a soothsayer, possessed (68:51), a magician (38:4). It was said that a man was teaching him (16:103) — the Qur'an answers that the one they point to speaks a foreign tongue, whereas the Qur'an is in clear Arabic. There was talk of "legends of the former peoples which he has written down, dictated to him morning and evening" (25:5).

What is nowhere to be found is: *"we saw him read"*. In a society where everyone knew everyone, the argument would have been unanswerable. It was never used.

## The content of the narratives

The Qur'an relates detailed episodes about Moses, Joseph, Mary, the People of the Cave, Dhu al-Qarnayn. Some overlap with the biblical tradition, others depart from it sharply, and the Qur'an owns those departures by explicitly correcting points accepted elsewhere.

The verse following the account of Mary and Zachariah is striking:

*"That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. And you were not with them when they cast their pens as to which of them should be responsible for Mary."* (Qur'an 3:44)

And after the account of Joseph:

*"That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. And you were not with them when they put together their plan while they conspired."* (Qur'an 12:102)

The text does not merely narrate: each time it underlines that the narrator was not a witness and had no access to the sources.

## The serious objection, and what can be said of it

The hypothesis of oral transmission deserves to be put frankly: Makkah was a caravan city, there were Christians and Jews in Arabia, narratives circulated.

Two elements weigh against it.

The first is **precision**. Second-hand oral transmission produces approximations, blendings, floating versions. The Qur'anic narratives are structured, coherent from one sura to another across twenty-three years, and detailed where one would not expect it.

The second is **correction**. A compiler reworks his sources; he does not contradict them head-on, least of all before communities that know them by heart and are waiting for a slip. The Qur'an corrects central points of the biblical account — and does so in Madinah, in the direct presence of literate Jewish tribes.

## A note on method

This argument, like the previous one, depends on no scientific discovery. It rests on historical data: what the opponents said and did not say, the nature of the narratives, the context of their transmission. That is firmer ground than the natural sciences, whose models change.

chapters.title: Vingt-trois ans sans contradiction
chapters.text:
## A book written under the least favourable conditions

The Qur'an was not composed. It was revealed in fragments over some twenty-three years, and those fragments answered circumstances that bore no resemblance to one another.

In Makkah: thirteen years of persecution, of boycott, of a despised minority. The suras there are short, hammered out, turned toward divine oneness, resurrection, responsibility.

In Madinah: ten years of an organised community, of treaties, battles, government. The passages lengthen and deal with inheritance, marriage, finance, war and peace.

Between the two: victories, reverses, bereavements, a public accusation levelled at the Prophet's ﷺ wife, the death of his son. No overall rereading was possible — each part was memorised and recited as soon as it was revealed, before the next existed.

The Qur'an points to this constraint as a test:

*"Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? If it had been from any other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction."* (Qur'an 4:82)

## What the constraint implies

An author who rereads himself can harmonise after the fact. Here there is nothing of the sort: the text is built in public, under pressure, with no possibility of going back. Each new revelation had to agree with everything that preceded it, on unrelated subjects, before opponents watching for the flaw.

This coherence is not merely the absence of contradiction. It is thematic too: divine oneness, individual responsibility, justice, recompense — these axes run through the whole without ever wavering, even as circumstances moved from extreme weakness to power.

## The passages that put the messenger in difficulty

One detail holds the attention: the Qur'an contains passages that **put the Prophet ﷺ in difficulty**.

The best known opens the sura *'Abasa*:

*"He frowned and turned away because there came to him the blind man."* (Qur'an 80:1-2)

The scene: the Prophet ﷺ was speaking with notables of Quraysh whom he hoped to convince when a blind companion, Ibn Umm Maktum, interrupted to ask a question. He showed irritation. The reproach came, and it stands in the text the community has recited ever since.

Other passages run the same way: a rebuke over the prisoners of Badr (8:67-68), another over a prohibition he had imposed on himself (66:1), a correction on a decision concerning the hypocrites (9:43).

There are also the silences. When his wife Aisha was publicly accused, the revelation clearing her came only after several weeks — weeks of anguish reported in detail in the hadith collections. A humanly composed text would have settled the matter at once.

These elements are hard to explain by self-interested authorship. They correspond exactly, on the other hand, to what one expects of a messenger who transmits what he receives, including when it concerns himself.

## Abrogation, an objection to address

Some verses modify earlier provisions — this is *naskh*. It is sometimes taken for contradiction. Yet the distinction is clear: a contradiction is asserting and denying the same thing at the same moment; abrogation is a prescription that develops in stages, each stage explicitly situated.

The prohibition of wine is the type case. It proceeds in three steps: first a qualified statement (2:219), then the prohibition of approaching prayer while intoxicated (4:43), finally the complete prohibition (5:90). A graduated pedagogy, applied to a society where drink was deeply entrenched — not a reversal.

The Qur'an in fact announces the principle itself (2:106), which a text seeking to conceal its inconsistencies would not do.

chapters.title: Un texte préservé
chapters.text:
## A promise that can be measured

*"Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian."* (Qur'an 15:9)

What is particular about this promise is that it is **verifiable**. Fourteen centuries have passed; one can look at what happened.

## Two channels rather than one

The transmission of the Qur'an rests on two parallel routes that check one another.

**Memorisation.** The text is learned by heart in full, with its rules of pronunciation, by a considerable number of people in each generation. A *hafiz* recites before a master who himself recited before his own, in an unbroken chain. Even today, millions carry the entire text in memory, in unrelated countries and languages.

**Writing.** Recording begins in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, with appointed scribes. Under the caliph Abu Bakr, after the battle of Yamama in which many memorisers died, a first compilation is established. Under Uthman, a reference copy is fixed and sent to the major centres.

This double channel is what makes the difference. A copying error is corrected by memory; a lapse of memory is corrected by the written text. Both would have had to drift together, everywhere, for the text to change.

## What the manuscripts say

This point is no longer a matter of conviction: very early fragments have been carbon-14 dated by university laboratories.

**The Birmingham manuscript.** Held at the University of Birmingham, it carries passages of suras 19 (*Maryam*) and 20 (*Ta-Ha*), written in ink in hijazi script. Dating places it between **568 and 645** of our era — a range that covers the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime and the decades immediately following.

**The Sanaa palimpsest.** Discovered in Yemen in 1972 during work at the Great Mosque, it bears two superimposed layers of writing. Datings place it before 646, some analyses reaching further back still.

**The corpus as a whole.** More than sixty fragments, totalling over two thousand folios, are attested as witnesses to the Qur'anic text earlier than the year 800.

Comparison is the decisive point: the Birmingham manuscript, the related folios held in Paris and the upper layer of the Sanaa palimpsest carry **the same textual type — the same words in the same order**. The differences noted concern verse division and diacritical marks, that is, conventions of writing, not content.

## What this establishes, and what it does not

One must stay exact.

These manuscripts establish that the text Muslims recite today corresponds to the one circulating in the very first decades of Islam. That is a remarkable historical result — few ancient texts have a documentary base so close to their origin, and so homogeneous.

They do not establish, on their own, the divine origin of the text: a text can be faithfully transmitted without that saying anything about its source. This is an argument about **preservation**, not about revelation.

But set against the promise of verse 15:9, the result carries weight: what was announced did in fact happen, and it can be measured.

chapters.title: La prophétie de Rome
chapters.text:
## An announcement against the grain

*"Alif, Lam, Mim. The Byzantines have been defeated in the nearest land. But they, after their defeat, will overcome within a few years. To Allah belongs the command before and after. And that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah."* (Qur'an 30:1-5)

To gauge how unexpected these verses are, one has to return to the situation.

## "In the nearest land"

One word in the verse deserves a pause: *fi adna l-ard*, rendered above as "in the nearest land".

*Adna* comes from the root *d-n-w*, which carries the idea of nearness — this is the sense the classical exegetes kept: the land nearest Arabia, as opposed to the distant regions of the empire. That reading is the principal one and is perfectly coherent.

The same root, however, carries a second sense, that of what is **low**, inferior. The word *dunya*, denoting the world here below, derives from it.

Now the decisive Byzantine defeats took place in the Syro-Palestinian region, around Jerusalem and the Jordan. And that region contains the **lowest point of all the emerged land on the globe**: the shore of the Dead Sea, about 430 metres below sea level. No other point of dry land on the planet is lower.

**How to take it.** One must be clear about the status of this reading: it is **modern**, it was not proposed by the early exegetes, and it rests on a secondary sense of the word. That is not how the verse was understood for thirteen centuries, and the altitude of the Dead Sea was measured only in the nineteenth century.

What can honestly be said: it is a resonance, not a demonstration. The primary sense — "the nearest land" — remains the sense of the verse. That the chosen word also carries the idea of lowness, and that geography lends itself to it, is a remarkable coincidence; to make a proof of it would be to force the text.

## The situation at the time of revelation

Two empires share the known world: the Byzantine empire, Christian, and the Sassanid Persian empire, Zoroastrian. For years the war has been going the Persians' way.

In **614** they take Jerusalem. The city is sacked, the True Cross carried off as a trophy. The shock across the Christian world is immense. The Byzantines lose Syria, Palestine, Egypt. The empire seems in its death throes; the emperor Heraclius considers, according to the chronicles, moving his capital to Carthage.

It is in this context that the text announces not only that the Byzantines will recover, but that they will do so *bid' sinin* — an Arabic expression denoting an interval of between three and nine years.

In Makkah, where Quraysh saw the Persian victory as an omen favourable to their own cause, the announcement was met with derision. The accounts report that Abu Bakr made a public wager with Ubayy ibn Khalaf on its fulfilment.

## What happened

**622**: Heraclius launches his counter-offensive and wins his first victories in Anatolia. This is the turn of the tide.

**627**: the battle of Nineveh breaks the Persian army.

**628**: the Sassanids capitulate.

**629**: the True Cross returns to Jerusalem.

## An honest discussion of the date

One point is debated and it is better to set it out than to pass over it.

Counting from the fall of Jerusalem (614) to the complete recovery (629) gives fifteen years — beyond the stated range. The objection is real.

The usual answer, and it holds: the verse announces that the Byzantines "will overcome", not that they will have completed the reconquest. Historians date the military reversal to **622** — it is Heraclius' campaign that marks the tipping point, after which the Byzantines advance without pause. From 614 to 622 we are indeed within the interval of three to nine years.

It remains that the calculation depends on the starting point chosen — which defeat exactly — and the end point — which victory counts. That is a matter of interpretation, not an exact measurement.

## What stands, whichever reading is taken

Even setting aside the question of years, the essential holds: **at the darkest moment for Byzantium, a text announces its recovery.** On that kind of forecast, a shrewd observer of the day would have bet the other way — and the Makkans did.

The verse adds a second element, often forgotten: *"and that day the believers will rejoice"*. The sources place the victory at Nineveh and that at Badr — or according to others, Hudaybiyya — in the same period, making the two rejoicings coincide.

## One announcement among others

This one has the advantage of bearing on facts historians document independently. But the Qur'an and the Sunnah contain others, riskier still because they name persons and set near deadlines — they are the subject of the next chapter.

chapters.title: Abû Lahab, Badr et les bracelets de Khosrô
chapters.text:
## Announcements that put their bearer at stake

The prophecy of Rome concerned two distant empires. Other announcements are far riskier: they name persons, specify places, set verifiable deadlines — and they were pronounced before opponents who wanted nothing more than a refutation.

## Abu Lahab: an announcement a single word would have ruined

Sura 111 names a living man — Abu Lahab, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle and one of his most determined opponents:

*"May the hands of Abu Lahab perish, and perish he. His wealth will not avail him or that which he gained. He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame, and his wife as well — the carrier of firewood."* (Qur'an 111:1-4)

The announcement is unambiguous: this man will die in refusal, and will not be saved.

It is revealed years before his death. Yet Abu Lahab had only one gesture to make in order to refute it publicly: to pronounce the profession of faith, even out of calculation, even without believing it. The text would have been caught out before all Makkah, on a clear point, unverifiable any other way.

He did not do it. He died in his opposition, a few years later.

## "The multitude will be defeated"

This verse was revealed in Makkah, in a sura of the Makkan period, when the Muslims were a handful of persecuted men, without arms or power:

*"The multitude will be defeated and will turn their backs."* (Qur'an 54:45)

Umar ibn al-Khattab himself reports his bafflement: when this verse came down, he wondered what multitude it could possibly mean. At the time the question was legitimate — no confrontation was in sight.

Al-Bukhari reports the scene at Badr, two years after the hijra. The Prophet ﷺ, under his shelter, was calling on his Lord insistently. Then he came out reciting this verse. Umar says he understood then what it had announced.

The Muslims, about three hundred, prevailed that day over an army three times their number.

## The return to Makkah

At the moment of leaving his city, driven out, hunted, not knowing whether he would ever see the Ka'ba again, the Prophet ﷺ receives this:

*"Indeed, He who imposed upon you the Qur'an will take you back to a place of return."* (Qur'an 28:85)

Eight years later he enters Makkah without a battle.

## The dream of Hudaybiyya

The episode is among the most trying in the prophetic biography. The Prophet ﷺ had seen in a dream the Muslims entering Makkah for the pilgrimage. They set out — and were turned back at Hudaybiyya, forced to sign a treaty on humiliating terms, and then to retrace their steps.

The dismay was real: several companions, Umar among them, were deeply troubled by it. It is in this context that there came down:

*"Certainly has Allah showed to His Messenger the vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in safety, with your heads shaved and hair shortened, not fearing anyone."* (Qur'an 48:27)

The announcement is maintained and made more precise at the very moment the facts seem to contradict it. It was fulfilled two years later.

## The bracelets of Khosrow

This announcement belongs to the Sunnah, and it has the advantage of being implausible at the moment it is spoken.

During the hijra, while the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr were fleeing Makkah, the horseman Suraqa ibn Malik gave chase to collect the bounty promised by Quraysh. His mount sank into the ground. He gave up, asked for quarter — and was told that he would one day wear **the bracelets of Khosrow**, the sovereign of the Persian empire.

The gap between the situation and the announcement is arresting: two fugitives hiding in the desert, and the evocation of the jewels of the most powerful monarch in the region.

Under the caliphate of Umar, the Sassanid empire collapses. When the royal treasure reaches Madinah, Umar summons Suraqa and slips the bracelets onto his wrists. The account is in al-Bukhari's *Sahih*.

## Al-Hasan and the reconciliation

The Prophet ﷺ once mounted the pulpit with his grandson al-Hasan and said, in the report transmitted by Abu Bakra in al-Bukhari's *Sahih*:

*"This son of mine is a master; perhaps Allah will reconcile through him two great groups of Muslims."*

The announcement presupposes something grave: that the community will split into two camps.

It was fulfilled in the year 41 of the hijra. After the first civil war, al-Hasan ibn Ali, then recognised as caliph, renounced power in favour of Mu'awiya to end the conflict. The year has stayed in history under the name *'am al-jama'a* — the year of the gathering.

## What these announcements have in common

They share three traits that set them apart from vague predictions.

They are **datable** — we know when they were spoken, and before whom. They are **falsifiable** — one gesture from Abu Lahab, a defeat at Badr, an al-Hasan dead young, and each of them collapses. And they were spoken **at the least favourable moment**: flight for the bracelets, expulsion for Hudaybiyya, extreme weakness for Badr.

It is this last point that strikes hardest. A man who invents promises frames them when they look plausible. These were all voiced when they seemed absurd.

chapters.title: Comment lire les versets de la création
chapters.text:
## The Qur'an calls us to look at the world

First, a fact: the Qur'an refers constantly to creation as an object of observation.

*"Do they not see the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings?"* (Qur'an 67:19)

*"So let man observe from what he was created."* (Qur'an 86:5)

*"We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth."* (Qur'an 41:53)

The word used is ***aya*** — the same as for "verse". The world and the text are presented as two books to be read. That invitation is constant, and it nourished centuries of science in the lands of Islam.

The chapters that follow work through verses describing the sky, the earth, the seas, the forming of the human being. Before entering them, the method must be set out — that is what separates a reading that holds from one that collapses.

## Two approaches not to be confused

Scholarly tradition distinguishes two things that are often mixed:

***Tafsir 'ilmi*** is a reading that illuminates a verse in the light of a scientific finding. It is an interpretation: it proposes, it does not impose, and it can be revised.

***I'jaz 'ilmi*** claims more: to establish that the verse contains information its age could not have known, and to draw from that a proof of divine origin. That requires certainty about the science — and certainty about the meaning of the verse.

Confusing the two is the source of most of the excesses.

## Four precautions

**1. The Qur'an is not a scientific treatise.** It never presents itself as one. Its purpose is guidance. To look for a manual in it is to mistake the book — and to attribute to it claims it does not make.

**2. Science moves, the Qur'an does not.** A verse does not draw its truth from the scientific model that illuminates it. If the model is revised — and that is the nature of science — it is the correspondence that falls, not the verse. Better, then, to rest a reading on what is established and durable than on the discovery of the month.

**3. Meaning comes first.** The exegetes' rule is firm: a verse is understood through the Arabic of the seventh century, through the context of revelation, through the other verses, through what the Prophet ﷺ and his companions said about it. A word cannot mean what none of its first hearers could have heard in it.

**4. An Arabic word often carries several senses.** When a verse seems to describe exactly some recent discovery, the sound course is to open the dictionary and set down every sense of the word, then see what the exegetes said. A reading that holds is one that stays true once all the senses are on the table.

## The rule followed in this book

The chapters that follow keep to verses whose **apparent sense, in the Arabic of the time, is already the one retained** — without needing to force a word. Where the correspondence is striking, it is flagged. Where several readings are possible, they are given.

One thing only is systematically set aside: **correspondences that depend on a translation**. When an effect works in English and vanishes in Arabic, it comes from the translator, not from the text.

**The case of the counts.** The Qur'an also lends itself to a reading of another order: that of numbers. How many times a letter recurs, where a word falls, how many letters make up a verse. The next chapter is devoted to it, and every result there is given with its calculation and the means to redo it yourself.

The criterion there is reproducibility: a count holds when two people who redo it separately, on the same text, find the same number.

## A better way to put the question

The soundest question is not: *"does the Qur'an contain scientific discoveries?"*

It is: *"how does a seventh-century Arabic text manage to speak of the natural world without taking up any of the cosmological errors of its time?"*

For that is what is striking. Late antiquity teemed with representations now abandoned: the earth carried on an animal, the sky held up by mountains, mythological explanations of phenomena. Those beliefs were everywhere — including in the Arabia where the Qur'an was revealed.

They are not found in the Qur'an. That silence is perhaps more remarkable than any particular correspondence.

chapters.title: Les comptages : refaites le calcul
chapters.text:
## What this chapter does

This chapter tells no story. It counts.

Here is what is at issue. The Qur'an is a text every word and every letter of which has been fixed for fourteen centuries: nothing has been moved, nothing added. That means it can be **counted** — counted for how many times a letter appears in it, where a word falls, how many letters make up a verse. And when you count, you find these numbers landing on values that mean something.

A few examples of what follows, to fix ideas:

- One letter recurs 1,273 times in the Qur'an, and its middle occurrence — the 637th — falls precisely on the sura that bears its name.
- The word "thunder" appears in only two verses, eleven suras apart, and those two verses are exactly the same size: same number of words, same number of letters.
- The formula by which Allah announces to the Prophet ﷺ his death appears only three times. Adding the numbers of those three suras gives the age at which he ﷺ died.

None of these numbers is visible on reading. You have to go through the 6,236 verses and keep count for them to appear.

## Two counting rules, and why they matter

Two things must be settled before counting anything, or two people will not arrive at the same number.

**What is counted.** Only the text of the verses — the 6,236. Sura titles are outside it: they are markers added for orientation, not revelation. Including them shifts the totals.

**How the text is written.** The Qur'an is written today in two ways. That of the mushaf, called *uthmani*, reproduces the ancient orthography. The simplified spelling, called *imla'i*, writes Arabic as it is commonly written today. Both say exactly the same text, but not always with the same number of characters — a word like صلاة is written صلوة in the mushaf.

That is why every count in this chapter was done **in both orthographies**, and the tables give both columns. When the two give the same number, the result owes nothing to a way of writing: it is in the text itself.

## Redoing the calculations yourself

After each result you will find the procedure. That is the point of this chapter: that nothing here rests on my word.

The first thing to obtain is the text of the Qur'an in a form a computer can read.

A photograph of a mushaf page will not do. To a computer, a photo is only a drawing: it distinguishes no letters in it and so can count nothing. What you need is **selectable text** — the kind you can highlight with the mouse, then copy and paste elsewhere. The test is immediate: if you can highlight a word, it is text; if nothing highlights, it is an image.

The sites [quran.com](https://quran.com) and [tanzil.net](https://tanzil.net) give the complete text in this form, in both orthographies.

A simple word processor is enough after that: the "Find" function in Word or LibreOffice displays how many times a letter appears in what you have selected. For the additions, a spreadsheet.

Three things to settle before starting:

- **ط and ظ are two distinct letters.** A badly configured search conflates them.
- **The vowel marks** (fatha, damma, kasra…) must not interfere with the search. The safest course is to use an unvocalised text.
- **The 112 basmalas** placed at the head of suras are not numbered verses, except in *Al-Fatiha*. They contain none of the letters studied here, so they change nothing — but it is as well to know.

## The median ط

**The claim.** The letter ط appears 1,273 times in the Qur'an, and the ط of **طه** — the first word of sura 20 — occupies exactly the middle: 636 before it, 636 after.

**The calculation.**

| | Uthmani | Imla'i |
|---|---|---|
| Total of ط | 1273 | 1273 |
| ط before 20:1 | 636 | 636 |
| ط after 20:1 | 636 | 636 |

636 + 1 + 636 = 1273. The ط of *Ta-Ha* is the 637th out of 1,273 — the exact median position. Both orthographies give the same result.

**What this requires.** For a letter to fall exactly in the middle, its total must be odd — otherwise there is no unique middle — and the central occurrence must sit somewhere remarkable. Of the twenty-eight letters of the Arabic alphabet, fifteen have an even total. Thirteen remain. For twelve of them, the median occurrence falls in the middle of a narrative, with nothing particular about it. Only one falls on the opening of a sura: ط — and on the one that bears its own letter.

**Redoing the calculation.** Count the ط from sura 1 through sura 19 inclusive: you will find 636. The next ط in the text is the very first character of sura 20. Then count from 20:1 to the end: 637, including the one in *Ta-Ha*.

## The disconnected letters read in base 19

**The claim.** Two verses announce that **Ta-Sin-Mim** are "the verses of the clear Book" (Qur'an 26:2 and 28:2). Counted across all the openings, these three letters give a number which, read in base 19, equals exactly the number of verses in the Qur'an.

**The calculation.** Twenty-nine suras open with disconnected letters. One point to note before counting: sura 42 is the only one to spread its letters over two verses — حم in verse 1, then عسق in verse 2.

Bringing the twenty-nine openings together gives 78 letters in all, drawn from 14 distinct letters. Among them:

| Letter | Occurrences in the openings |
|---|---|
| ط | 4 |
| س | 5 |
| م | 17 |

Arabic being written from right to left, the three numbers are placed in the order of the letters: **17 | 5 | 4**. Read in base 19:

17 × 19² + 5 × 19 + 4 = 6137 + 95 + 4 = **6236**

That is the number of verses in the Qur'an — what the two verses announced.

**Redoing the calculation.** Note the openings of the 29 suras concerned: 2, 3, 7, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 19, 20, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 36, 38, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 50 and 68. Count the ط, the س and the م. Do not forget the عسق of 42:2.

## The 114 suras split into two halves

**The claim.** Adding, for each sura, its rank and its number of verses yields an exact division into two halves that answer one another.

**The calculation.** Take the 114 suras. For each, form the sum: *rank + number of verses*. Sura 1 has 7 verses, so 1 + 7 = 8, an even number. Sura 2 has 286 verses, so 2 + 286 = 288, even. Sura 3 has 200 verses, so 3 + 200 = 203, odd. And so on to 114.

Now separate the suras into two groups according to whether this total is even or odd:

| | Number of suras | Sum of (rank + verses) |
|---|---|---|
| **Even** group | 57 | **6236** |
| **Odd** group | 57 | **6555** |

Three results can be read in this table:

- The split falls at **57 and 57** — exactly half of 114, when nothing required it.
- The sum of the even group is **6236**, the total number of verses in the Qur'an.
- The sum of the odd group is **6555**, which is 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 114, the sum of all the ranks.

The heart of the result states itself in one line. Since the overall total is 6236 + 6555, saying that the even group gives 6236 amounts to saying this:

> The sum of the **ranks** of the 57 suras in the even group equals the sum of the **verses** of the 57 suras in the odd group.

Both come to **3303**.

**Redoing the calculation.** All you need is the list of the 114 suras with their verse counts, as found in any mushaf, and a spreadsheet. Three columns: the rank, the number of verses, and their sum. A fourth column marks whether that sum is even. Then total each group.

## The table of four cells

**The claim.** Let us classify the 114 suras by two criteria only: is the rank even or odd, and is the number of verses even or odd. The four cells obtained do not fill at random.

**The calculation.** Rank first divides the book into two equal halves: 57 suras of even rank, 57 of odd rank. Now let us count, in each half, those whose number of verses is even:

| | Even number of verses | Odd number of verses | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Suras of **even** rank | **30** | **27** | 57 |
| Suras of **odd** rank | **30** | **27** | 57 |
| Total | 60 | 54 | 114 |

The two halves divide **in exactly the same way**: 30 and 27 on either side. Nothing required this symmetry — the number of verses in a sura has no bearing on the parity of its rank.

What is particular about this count is that it leaves no room for choice: you take the 114 suras, apply two criteria each with only two possible answers, and fill the table. There is nothing to select.

**Redoing the calculation.** The list of the 114 suras with their verse counts is enough. In a spreadsheet, one column for the parity of the rank, one for the parity of the verse count, then a cross-count.

## The 6,236 verses cut into two equal halves

**The claim.** Every verse of the Qur'an carries two numbers: that of its sura and its own. Let us simply compare whether these two numbers have the **same parity** — both even, or both odd.

**The calculation.** Take verse 3 of sura 5: 5 is odd, 3 is odd — the parities agree. Verse 4 of sura 5: 5 is odd, 4 is even — they disagree. Classify the 6,236 verses of the book this way, one by one.

| | Number of verses |
|---|---|
| **Agreeing** parities (odd-odd or even-even) | **3,118** |
| **Disagreeing** parities | **3,118** |
| Total | 6,236 |

The two groups are **exactly equal** — 3,118 each, precisely half of 6,236.

This is the barest count in the chapter. It bears on no word, no letter, no numerical value: only on the two numbers each verse carries. Nothing is chosen, nothing left aside; the whole book is classified. And the split falls at the exact middle.

**Redoing the calculation.** Two ways, which must give the same number. The most direct: go through the 6,236 verses and count those whose two numbers share parity. The quickest, in a spreadsheet: for each sura of rank *n* with *v* verses, it contains (*v*+1)÷2 verses of odd number rounded down, and *v*÷2 of even number. Depending on whether *n* is odd or even, add one or the other to the total. The sum is 3,118.

## The name of Noah

**The claim.** The name of Nuh (نوح) is cited 43 times in the Qur'an, and that number 43 reappears in the structure of the book.

**The calculation.** The sura *Nuh* holds rank **71** and has **28** verses.

| What is counted | Result |
|---|---|
| Occurrences of the name نوح | **43** |
| Suras mentioning it | **28** |
| Last sura to mention it | **71** |
| Suras after the 71st that mention it | **0** |
| Suras among the first 70 that do not mention it | **43** |

And the arithmetic of the ranks:

- 71 − 28 = **43** — the rank of the sura minus its number of verses.
- 114 − 71 = **43** — the number of suras following sura *Nuh*, none of which names him.

The number of suras mentioning him, **28**, is also the number of verses in his sura.

**A point to know in order to count correctly.** In the orthography of the mushaf, four of these occurrences are fused with the vocative particle — يٰنوح, "O Nuh" (11:32, 11:46, 11:48 and 26:116). A search set on the isolated word will not see them. The total is indeed **43** in both orthographies, provided this form is included in the search.

**Redoing the calculation.** Search for نوح in the complete text, taking care to include the prefixed forms (ونوح, لنوح) and the attached vocative form يٰنوح. Note the suras: you will find 28, the last being the 71st.

## The three verses of the summons

**The claim.** The Qur'an addresses the Prophet ﷺ announcing his death by a precise verb form: *natawaffayannaka*, "We will surely cause you to die". This form appears only three times, and the ranks of those three suras added together give the age at which he ﷺ died.

**The calculation.** Searching for نتوفينك in the complete text gives exactly three occurrences, with no other variant of this form:

| Verse | Sura | Rank |
|---|---|---|
| 10:46 | Yunus | 10 |
| 13:40 | Ar-Ra'd | 13 |
| 40:77 | Ghafir | 40 |

10 + 13 + 40 = **63**

The Prophet ﷺ died at the age of sixty-three — the age is reported in *Sahih al-Bukhari* and *Sahih Muslim*.

This count has a quality the others do not always have: the selection rule leaves no latitude. You do not choose the verses; the verb form designates them, and you take all three.

**Redoing the calculation.** Search for the string نتوفينك in the complete Arabic text. You will get these three verses and no others. Add the numbers of their suras.

## The two verses of thunder

**The claim.** The word *ar-ra'd*, thunder, appears in only two verses of the Qur'an, and those two verses are exactly the same size.

**The calculation.** Searching the word gives two verses, and only two: **2:19** and **13:13**.

| | Words | Letters (uthmani) | Letters (imla'i) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2:19 | 19 | 83 | 86 |
| 13:13 | 19 | 83 | 86 |

Both verses have **19 words** each, and the same number of letters. The letter total depends on the orthography — 83 in the mushaf's, 86 in the simplified one — but **the equality between the two verses holds in both cases**. It is the equality that makes the result, and it depends on no way of writing.

**And there is more.** The Arabic word for thunder, *ra'd*, is written with three letters: ر ع د. Let us count how many times these three letters appear inside each of the two verses:

| | ر | ع | د | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2:19 | 4 | 4 | 1 | **9** |
| 13:13 | 2 | 2 | 5 | **9** |

Nine in one, nine in the other — although the distribution is quite different: the first verse is loaded with ر and ع, the second with د. These are two different routes to the same total, and it holds in both orthographies.

**Redoing the calculation.** Search for رعد in the complete text: you will get only these two verses. Count the words of each, then the letters with the spaces removed. For the second table, count in each verse the occurrences of ر, then ع, then د.

## The refrain of Ar-Rahman

**The claim.** The sura *Ar-Rahman* is run through by a question returning like a refrain: *"So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?"* It returns 31 times, and the numbers of those 31 verses behave in a singular way.

**The calculation.** The refrain occupies the following verses of sura 55:

13, 16, 18, 21, 23, 25, 28, 30, 32, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42, 45, 47, 49, 51, 53, 55, 57, 59, 61, 63, 65, 67, 69, 71, 73, 75, 77

They are **31** — and 31 is a prime number, divisible only by itself and 1. Now let us add these numbers, then their squares, their cubes, their fourth powers:

| Operation | Result | Prime? |
|---|---|---|
| Sum of the numbers | 1,433 | yes |
| Sum of the squares | 77,201 | yes |
| Sum of the cubes | 4,567,151 | yes |
| Sum of the fourth powers | 286,406,069 | yes |

All four sums are prime, and their count is prime too. Five conditions, all met.

A number taken at random around 1,433 has about a one-in-seven chance of being prime; around 286 million, about one in twenty. That all four should fall together is not what one expects from an ordinary list of numbers.

**Redoing the calculation.** Note the numbers of the verses carrying the refrain in sura 55 — they are easy to spot, the verse being identical each time. A spreadsheet gives the four sums; for testing the primality of the large numbers, online calculators will do.

## Al-Fatiha and the number 19

**The claim.** *Al-Fatiha* is sura no. 1 and has 7 verses, numbered 1 to 7. Writing the sura's rank followed by its verse numbers side by side gives a number divisible by 19.

**The calculation.** The rank, then the seven numbers:

**1** | 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 → **11,234,567**

11,234,567 ÷ 19 = **591,293**, with no remainder.

**Redoing the calculation.** A calculator is enough. Note that all seven verses are needed: removing one or adding one loses the divisibility.

## The numerical value of iron

**The claim.** In the *abjad* system, where each Arabic letter carries a numerical value fixed long ago, the word حديد (iron) gives the atomic number of iron.

**The calculation.** The abjad values of the letters concerned:

| Letter | ا | ل | ح | د | ي |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Value | 1 | 30 | 8 | 4 | 10 |

**حديد** = ح (8) + د (4) + ي (10) + د (4) = **26**

26 is the atomic number of iron, that is, its number of protons — a quantity depending on no unit of measurement and no convention: it is a count of objects.

With the definite article:

**الحديد** = ا (1) + ل (30) + ح (8) + د (4) + ي (10) + د (4) = **57**

57 is the rank of the sura *Al-Hadid* — *The Iron*.

**Redoing the calculation.** The full abjad table is published everywhere and has not varied. Add the values of the letters, without counting the vocalisation or the shadda.

## What these calculations have in common

Each of these results rests on a simple rule, laid down before counting and applied to the end: every occurrence of a letter, every verse containing a word, every sura in the book. Nothing is chosen along the way.

And each can be redone with a text, a spreadsheet and a little patience. Two people taking them up separately arrive at the same numbers.

These arrangements run through a text of 6,236 verses, revealed over twenty-three years, at a time when neither the zero, nor base-19 arithmetic, nor any means of enumerating the letters of an entire book was available. They have been there, in the Book, for fourteen centuries — and it is enough to count to see them.

chapters.title: Le ciel et l'origine de l'univers
chapters.text:
## Une origine commune

*« Ceux qui ont mécru n'ont-ils pas vu que les cieux et la terre formaient une masse compacte (ratq) ? Ensuite Nous les avons séparés (fataq) et fait de l'eau toute chose vivante. Ne croiront-ils donc pas ? »* (Coran 21:30)

Les deux mots sont précis en arabe. *Ratq* désigne ce qui est cousu, soudé, d'un seul tenant. *Fataq* désigne l'action de découdre, de fendre ce qui était joint.

Le verset énonce donc : les cieux et la terre formaient un tout, puis ont été séparés.

Cette représentation ne correspond à aucune cosmologie répandue au VIIᵉ siècle. Le modèle dominant, hérité d'Aristote et de Ptolémée, tenait l'univers pour éternel et immuable — une idée qui a dominé jusqu'au XXᵉ siècle. Ce n'est qu'avec les travaux de Lemaître et Hubble, puis la découverte du fond diffus cosmologique en 1965, que le modèle d'un univers ayant une origine s'est imposé.

Le verset n'est pas un exposé de physique : il n'énonce ni densité initiale, ni chronologie. Il énonce autre chose, et de plus tranchant. Là où toute la pensée savante de l'époque tenait le cosmos pour éternel, il affirme une origine et une séparation. C'est cette affirmation-là que la science a fini par rejoindre, treize siècles plus tard.

## Une expansion

*« Et le ciel, Nous l'avons construit par Notre puissance : et Nous l'étendons (mûsi'ûn) constamment dans l'immensité. »* (Coran 51:47)

Le mot *mûsi'ûn* vient de la racine *w-s-'*, qui porte l'idée d'élargir, d'étendre, de rendre vaste. La forme employée est un participe actif : une action en cours, non achevée.

Les exégètes anciens, n'ayant aucune notion d'expansion cosmique, l'ont lu dans le sens de l'ampleur et de la puissance — une lecture parfaitement recevable. La correspondance avec l'expansion de l'univers, établie par Hubble en 1929, s'ajoute à cette lecture sans l'annuler.

## Sept cieux

*« C'est Lui qui a créé pour vous tout ce qui est sur la terre, puis Il s'est adressé au ciel et en a fait sept cieux. »* (Coran 2:29)

L'expression revient plusieurs fois, et les exégètes en ont donné des lectures diverses — sept sphères, sept degrés, sept domaines du monde supérieur. Aucune de ces lectures n'a été close, et le verset garde sa part de mystère. Il est plus juste de le laisser ouvert que de lui assigner d'autorité un découpage moderne.

## Les orbites

*« C'est Lui qui a créé la nuit et le jour, le soleil et la lune, chacun voguant dans une orbite (falak). »* (Coran 21:33)

Le mot *falak* désigne en arabe une trajectoire circulaire, un cercle. Il se distingue de termes qui auraient simplement dit « chemin » ou « course ».

Deux éléments méritent d'être relevés. D'abord, le verset attribue un mouvement propre au **soleil**, là où la représentation courante lui prêtait une course apparente autour d'une terre fixe. Ensuite, le verbe employé, *yasbahûn*, évoque une nage — un mouvement libre dans un milieu, non un objet fixé sur une sphère solide, comme le supposaient les modèles à sphères concentriques de l'Antiquité.

Le soleil se déplace effectivement : il entraîne le système solaire autour du centre de la Voie lactée, à une vitesse estimée entre 220 et 240 km/s selon les méthodes de mesure.

## Deux mots différents pour deux astres

Le Coran ne désigne jamais la lumière du soleil et celle de la lune par le même mot.

*« C'est Lui qui a fait du soleil une clarté (diyâ') et de la lune une lumière (nûr). »* (Coran 10:5)

*« Et Il y a fait de la lune une lumière (nûr) et du soleil une lampe (sirâj). »* (Coran 71:16)

*« Béni soit Celui qui a placé au ciel des constellations, et y a placé une lampe (sirâj) et une lune éclairante (qamaran munîran). »* (Coran 25:61)

La distinction est constante. Le soleil est *sirâj* — une lampe, un luminaire qui brûle — ou *diyâ'*, une clarté intense, et ailleurs *wahhâj*, « ardent ». La lune est *nûr*, ou *munîr*, « qui éclaire ».

En arabe, *sirâj* évoque une source qui produit sa lumière en se consumant, comme une lampe à huile : chaleur et lumière ensemble. *Nûr* désigne la lumière en général, sans indiquer d'où elle vient.

Le vocabulaire distingue donc nettement un astre qui brûle d'un astre qui éclaire — et cela correspond à ce que nous savons : le soleil produit son rayonnement par fusion nucléaire, la lune renvoie celui qu'elle reçoit.

Ce qui frappe ici n'est pas un mot isolé mais une **constance**, et elle se vérifie sur l'ensemble du texte. Trois passages associent les astres à un mot de lumière — 10:5, 25:61 et 71:16 — et l'attribution n'y varie jamais :

| | Soleil | Lune |
|---|---|---|
| 10:5 | *diyâ'* (clarté) | *nûr* |
| 25:61 | *sirâj* (lampe) | *munîr* (qui éclaire) |
| 71:16 | *sirâj* (lampe) | *nûr* |

Le mot *sirâj* revient encore en 78:13 pour le soleil — *sirâjan wahhâjan*, « une lampe ardente ». Dans tout le Coran, la lune n'est jamais appelée *sirâj*, et le soleil n'est jamais appelé *nûr*. Sur vingt-trois ans de révélation, l'attribution ne se dément pas une seule fois.

## La nuit dont on retire le jour

*« Et un signe pour eux est la nuit : Nous en écorchons le jour, et les voilà dans les ténèbres. »* (Coran 36:37)

Le verbe employé, *naslakhu*, mérite qu'on s'y arrête. La racine *s-l-kh* signifie proprement **écorcher** — retirer la peau d'une bête. C'est un mot concret, presque brutal, et le Coran l'applique au passage du jour à la nuit.

La formulation inverse ce que l'expérience courante suggère. On dirait spontanément que la nuit tombe *sur* le jour ; ici, c'est le jour qu'on retire *de* la nuit, comme une peau qu'on ôte pour découvrir ce qu'il y a dessous. Les exégètes classiques l'avaient relevé : ôter une couverture fait apparaître ce qui était masqué — l'obscurité étant l'état de fond.

La physique donne raison à cette image. La clarté du jour n'est pas une substance : c'est de la lumière solaire **diffusée par l'atmosphère**. Une mince pellicule d'air qui disperse les courtes longueurs d'onde et donne au ciel son bleu. Retirez l'atmosphère, et la clarté disparaît avec elle.

C'est vérifiable ailleurs que sur Terre. Sur la Lune, dépourvue d'atmosphère, il n'y a pas de ciel bleu : en pleine journée lunaire, sous un Soleil éclatant, le ciel reste **noir et les étoiles visibles**. Les photographies prises depuis la Station spatiale montrent la même chose depuis l'extérieur — le jour y apparaît comme une fine couche bleutée posée sur le globe, entourée de noir.

Deux autres versets emploient un verbe complémentaire, *yughshî* — couvrir, envelopper :

*« Il couvre le jour de la nuit qui le poursuit sans arrêt. »* (Coran 7:54)

*« … et Il couvre le jour de la nuit. »* (Coran 13:3)

C'est le même rapport, énoncé dans l'autre sens : la nuit enveloppe, le jour est enveloppé. Vu depuis l'orbite, c'est littéralement ce qu'on observe — une mince pellicule lumineuse sur le globe, entourée de noir de toutes parts.

Le point ne tient à aucune interprétation forcée : il tient au **choix des verbes**. L'un traite le jour comme une peau que l'on retire, l'autre comme une chose que l'on enveloppe. C'est exactement ce qu'est la clarté du jour — une pellicule d'air illuminée, posée sur un globe, et que l'on ôte pour retrouver le noir qui était là dessous.

## Le ciel comme toit protecteur

*« Et Nous avons fait du ciel un toit protégé (saqfan mahfûzan). Et ils se détournent de ses merveilles. »* (Coran 21:32)

L'atmosphère remplit effectivement une fonction de protection : elle filtre les rayonnements ultraviolets et les rayons cosmiques, elle désintègre l'immense majorité des météorites, et le champ magnétique terrestre dévie le vent solaire.

Il faut noter que l'idée d'un ciel-toit existait dans les cosmologies anciennes. La particularité du verset tient à la qualification — *mahfûz*, « protégé », ou « qui préserve » — et à l'invitation qui suit : regarder ce dont on se détourne.

## Ce qu'il faut retenir

Aucun de ces versets ne se présente comme un énoncé scientifique, et aucun n'a été compris ainsi pendant treize siècles. Ce qu'ils ont en commun est plus discret et, à bien y regarder, plus solide : **ils ne contiennent aucune des erreurs que leur époque tenait pour évidentes.**

Ni terre plate, ni ciel porté par des colonnes, ni sphères solides, ni univers éternel. Dans un texte du VIIᵉ siècle qui parle abondamment du ciel, cette absence mérite d'être remarquée.

chapters.title: La terre, les montagnes et les mers
chapters.text:
## Les montagnes comme piquets

*« N'avons-Nous pas fait de la terre une couche ? Et des montagnes des piquets (awtâd) ? »* (Coran 78:6-7)

*« Et Il a implanté des montagnes immobiles dans la terre afin qu'elle ne branle pas en vous emportant. »* (Coran 16:15)

Le mot *watad* (pluriel *awtâd*) désigne le piquet que l'on enfonce en terre pour tenir une tente — objet familier à tout Bédouin. Sa caractéristique essentielle : **la partie enfouie est plus grande que la partie visible**, et c'est elle qui assure la stabilité.

La géologie a établi que les massifs montagneux possèdent effectivement une racine crustale profonde, souvent bien plus étendue que leur relief apparent, et que cette racine assure leur équilibre par flottaison sur le manteau — c'est le principe d'isostasie, dégagé au XIXᵉ siècle.

Le verset dit que les montagnes empêchent la terre de « branler » en nous emportant. C'est bien de la stabilité d'ensemble de la croûte qu'il s'agit : les racines montagneuses ancrent les plaques et équilibrent leur flottaison sur le manteau. L'image du piquet est donc juste jusque dans son détail — ce qui tient n'est pas ce qui dépasse, c'est ce qui est enfoncé.

## Des montagnes qui se déplacent

*« Et tu vois les montagnes, que tu crois figées, alors qu'elles passent comme des nuages. »* (Coran 27:88)

Le contexte du verset est eschatologique — il évoque le Jour de la Résurrection. Mais la formulation retient l'attention : elle dit que ce que nous *croyons* immobile ne l'est pas.

La tectonique des plaques, établie dans les années 1960, décrit précisément cela : les continents dérivent de quelques centimètres par an, entraînant les massifs.

Les deux niveaux se superposent sans se gêner : le sens premier, qui vise le Jour de la Résurrection, et une formulation qui se trouve décrire aussi l'état présent du monde.

## Deux mers qui ne se mélangent pas

*« Il a fait confluer les deux mers qui se rencontrent. Il y a entre elles une barrière (barzakh) qu'elles ne dépassent pas. »* (Coran 55:19-20)

*« Et c'est Lui qui a fait confluer les deux mers : l'une douce et agréable, l'autre salée et amère. Et Il a établi entre elles une barrière et un barrage infranchissable. »* (Coran 25:53)

L'océanographie a décrit ce phénomène : lorsque deux masses d'eau de salinité, de température et de densité différentes se rencontrent, elles ne se mélangent pas immédiatement. Une zone de transition — les océanographes parlent de front, de pycnocline, d'halocline — les sépare, et chacune conserve durablement ses propriétés.

C'est particulièrement visible au détroit de Gibraltar, où l'eau méditerranéenne, plus salée et plus dense, s'écoule sous l'eau atlantique en conservant ses caractéristiques sur des centaines de kilomètres. On l'observe aussi aux embouchures de grands fleuves, où l'eau douce se maintient au-dessus de l'eau salée avant de se diluer.

Ce phénomène est perceptible de surface — la différence de couleur est parfois visible à l'œil nu — mais son mécanisme, lui, n'a été compris qu'avec les mesures modernes de densité et de salinité.

## Les ténèbres des profondeurs

*« Ou [elles sont] comme des ténèbres dans une mer profonde : une vague le couvre, sur laquelle une autre vague, sur laquelle sont des nuages. Ténèbres les unes au-dessus des autres. Quand quelqu'un sort sa main, il ne la distingue presque pas. »* (Coran 24:40)

Le verset est une comparaison — il illustre l'état de celui qui s'écarte de la lumière de la foi. Mais sa description physique est exacte sur trois points.

**L'obscurité croissante.** L'eau absorbe les couleurs les unes après les autres, en commençant par les grandes longueurs d'onde : le rouge s'éteint vers quinze mètres, puis l'orange, le jaune, le vert. Le bleu descend le plus bas. La zone éclairée s'arrête vers 200 mètres ; entre 200 et 1 000 mètres s'étend la zone crépusculaire ; en dessous, l'obscurité est complète.

**Les vagues superposées.** Le verset distingue une vague, puis une autre au-dessus. L'océanographie décrit effectivement des **vagues internes**, qui se propagent en profondeur à l'interface entre deux couches d'eau de densités différentes — la pycnocline —, sous les vagues de surface.

Leurs dimensions sont considérables : des amplitudes de quelques dizaines de mètres, atteignant la centaine dans les zones les plus actives, pour des longueurs d'onde de plusieurs kilomètres. Et pourtant elles sont **invisibles depuis un navire** : rien n'apparaît en surface qu'une faible modulation, imperceptible à l'œil. C'est ce qui explique qu'on ne les ait caractérisées qu'avec l'imagerie satellitaire, à partir des années 1960, puis récemment avec des missions altimétriques dédiées.

**Les couches de ténèbres.** L'expression « ténèbres les unes au-dessus des autres » correspond à la stratification lumineuse par absorption successive des longueurs d'onde.

Un plongeur en apnée du VIIᵉ siècle ne descendait pas assez profond pour observer cela. C'est un domaine resté inaccessible jusqu'aux submersibles.

## Le fer « fait descendre »

*« Nous avons fait descendre le fer, dans lequel il y a une force redoutable, ainsi que des utilités pour les gens. »* (Coran 57:25)

Le verbe *anzalnâ* — « Nous avons fait descendre » — est celui employé pour la révélation et pour la pluie.

L'astrophysique établit que le fer ne se forme pas dans une étoile ordinaire comme notre soleil. Il marque le terme de la fusion productrice d'énergie : au-delà du fer, fusionner des noyaux consomme de l'énergie au lieu d'en libérer. Seules les étoiles très massives atteignent le stade où leur cœur produit du fer — et lorsque ce cœur se forme, plus rien ne soutient l'étoile, qui s'effondre. La supernova qui suit disperse le fer dans l'espace ; une autre part provient des supernovas de type Ia.

Dans tous les cas, le fer présent sur Terre s'est formé **avant** le système solaire, dans des étoiles mortes depuis longtemps, et faisait partie du nuage à partir duquel notre planète s'est constituée.

Les exégètes classiques ont majoritairement compris *anzalnâ* au sens de « Nous avons accordé, octroyé » — car le verbe porte aussi ce sens en arabe. Cette lecture reste entière. Elle n'empêche pas de remarquer que le mot choisi est celui de la descente — et que le fer, dont notre planète a hérité d'étoiles mortes avant elle, est bel et bien venu du ciel.

chapters.title: La création de l'être humain
chapters.text:
## Les étapes décrites

*« Nous avons certes créé l'homme d'un extrait d'argile. Puis Nous en fîmes une goutte (nutfa) dans un réceptacle sûr. Puis de cette goutte Nous créâmes une adhérence ('alaqa) ; puis de cette adhérence Nous créâmes un morceau mâché (mudgha) ; puis de ce morceau Nous créâmes des os ('izâm) ; puis Nous revêtîmes les os de chair. Puis Nous en fîmes une création autre. Béni soit Allah, le meilleur des créateurs ! »* (Coran 23:12-14)

Ce passage est le plus détaillé du Coran sur la formation de l'être humain. Il énonce une succession d'états, chacun nommé par un mot arabe précis.

## Les mots, un par un

***Nutfa*** — de la racine *n-t-f*, qui désigne une petite quantité de liquide, une goutte qui reste dans un récipient qu'on a vidé. Le Coran précise ailleurs *nutfa amchâj*, « une goutte mélangée » (76:2), ce qui suggère une composition et non un élément simple.

***'Alaqa*** — le mot le plus commenté. La racine *'-l-q* porte trois sens en arabe classique : ce qui **s'accroche, adhère** à quelque chose ; la **sangsue** ; le **caillot** de sang. Les trois sens sont attestés dans les dictionnaires anciens.

L'embryologie décrit qu'au terme de la première semaine, le blastocyste **s'implante** dans la muqueuse utérine et s'y accroche. Sa forme à ce stade, et sa relation nourricière au tissu maternel, ont été rapprochées de l'image de la sangsue. Le sang y est également très présent dans les lacunes du trophoblaste.

Ce qui est notable ici, c'est que les trois sens du mot correspondent à trois aspects réels du même stade — l'adhérence, la forme, le sang. Le sens premier, celui que retient l'essentiel des exégètes, est celui de l'adhérence : c'est aussi celui qui décrit le plus exactement ce qui se produit.

***Mudgha*** — littéralement « une bouchée mâchée », ce qui a été mastiqué. Au stade somitique, l'embryon présente une série de blocs segmentaires en relief, qui donnent à sa surface un aspect irrégulier — l'image de la matière marquée par des dents a été relevée par plusieurs auteurs.

***'Izâm* puis *lahm*** — les os, puis la chair qui les revêt. Cette séquence a été discutée : elle correspond à ce que décrit l'embryologie, la chondrification et l'ossification du squelette précédant le développement de la musculature qui vient l'entourer.

***« Une création autre »*** — la formule marque un saut qualitatif, non une étape de plus dans la même série.

## Ce que cette description a d'inhabituel pour son époque

La médecine grecque, qui faisait autorité, tenait des positions différentes. Aristote soutenait que l'embryon se formait à partir du sang menstruel coagulé par la semence masculine. Galien, plus tard, admettait une contribution des deux parents, mais dans un cadre humoral.

Aucune de ces théories ne décrit une implantation, ni une succession d'états morphologiques distincts. Le Coran, lui, ne reprend aucune des explications savantes disponibles.

## Le sexe et l'ascendance

*« C'est Lui qui a créé les deux éléments de couple, le mâle et la femelle, d'une goutte de sperme quand elle est éjectée. »* (Coran 53:45-46)

Le verset rattache la détermination du sexe à la *nutfa* — au liquide séminal. La génétique a établi que le sexe est déterminé par le chromosome porté par le spermatozoïde, X ou Y.

Il faut noter que la question était disputée dans l'Antiquité, avec des théories attribuant le rôle déterminant à la mère, à la température, ou au côté de l'utérus.

**Un second passage, et un point de grammaire.** La sourate 75 reprend la même affirmation, et sa formulation mérite attention :

*« N'était-il pas une goutte de sperme éjaculé ? Puis il fut une adhérence. Alors Il le créa et lui donna une forme harmonieuse. Puis Il en fit (fa-ja'ala **min-hu**) les deux éléments du couple, le mâle et la femelle. »* (Coran 75:37-39)

Le pronom employé au verset 39 est *min-hu* — « à partir **de lui** », au masculin. Or les trois termes candidats du passage n'ont pas le même genre en arabe : *nutfa* (la goutte) est **féminin**, *'alaqa* (l'adhérence) est **féminine**, et seul *maniyyin yumnâ* (le sperme éjaculé) est **masculin**.

La grammaire désigne donc sans ambiguïté ce à quoi le pronom renvoie : c'est du sperme, et de lui seul, que procède la détermination du sexe. Un féminin — *min-hâ* — aurait renvoyé à la goutte ou à l'adhérence.

Ce détail ne dépend d'aucun comptage ni d'aucune unité : il se lit dans l'accord des mots.

## D'entre le dos et les côtes

*« Que l'homme considère donc de quoi il a été créé ! Il a été créé d'une eau jaillissante, sortie d'entre le dos (as-sulb) et les côtes (at-tarâ'ib). »* (Coran 86:5-7)

Le verset pose une question — de quoi l'homme est-il fait ? — et y répond en situant l'origine de cette eau **entre la colonne vertébrale et les côtes**, c'est-à-dire dans la région lombaire, à hauteur du bas du thorax.

L'indication a longtemps paru étrange, car l'appareil qui produit le sperme se trouve ailleurs, bien plus bas. Les exégètes ont proposé plusieurs lectures de *tarâ'ib* — les côtes, le haut du buste.

L'embryologie a montré que le lieu désigné est le bon. Les gonades — testicules chez l'homme, ovaires chez la femme — **ne se forment pas là où on les trouve chez l'adulte**. Elles apparaissent chez l'embryon sur la paroi postérieure de l'abdomen, dans ce qu'on appelle la crête génitale, à hauteur des premières vertèbres lombaires : exactement entre la colonne et les côtes. Les testicules amorcent ensuite une longue descente et n'atteignent le scrotum qu'en fin de grossesse.

Et le lien avec le point de départ n'est jamais rompu. Ils gardent toute leur vie les vaisseaux, les nerfs et les vaisseaux lymphatiques de leur région d'origine : l'artère qui les irrigue naît de l'aorte abdominale à hauteur des lombes, et leur drainage remonte vers les ganglions situés le long de cette même aorte, et non vers l'aine pourtant voisine. C'est une donnée d'anatomie que les médecins utilisent tous les jours — une douleur testiculaire peut se ressentir dans l'abdomen, pour cette raison précise.

L'organe a donc bien son origine, et garde ses attaches, entre le dos et les côtes.

## L'empreinte digitale

*« L'homme pense-t-il que Nous ne réunirons jamais ses os ? Mais si ! Nous sommes capables de remodeler ses phalanges (banân). »* (Coran 75:3-4)

Le verset évoque la résurrection. Ce qui a retenu l'attention, c'est le choix du détail : parmi tout ce qu'on pourrait mentionner du corps, le texte désigne l'extrémité des doigts.

L'unicité des empreintes digitales n'a été établie qu'à la fin du XIXᵉ siècle, avec les travaux de Galton, et adoptée comme méthode d'identification à partir de 1892.

Le verset parle de phalanges, non d'empreintes. Mais la question qu'il pose est bien celle de l'identité : comment retrouver un homme parmi tous les autres après que ses os se sont dispersés. Et c'est précisément à l'extrémité des doigts que se trouve ce qui, chez l'être humain, n'appartient qu'à lui seul.

## La peau et la douleur

*« Ceux qui ont rejeté Nos signes, Nous les brûlerons dans un Feu. Chaque fois que leurs peaux auront été consumées, Nous leur donnerons d'autres peaux en échange afin qu'ils goûtent le châtiment. »* (Coran 4:56)

Le verset traite du châtiment dans l'au-delà — c'est son objet, et il ne prétend pas décrire une physiologie.

Ce qui a retenu l'attention est la logique qu'il suppose : le renouvellement de la peau y est présenté comme la condition pour que la douleur continue d'être ressentie. Autrement dit, la peau est le siège de la sensation.

La neurophysiologie le confirme. Les récepteurs de la douleur — les **nocicepteurs** — sont des terminaisons nerveuses libres densément réparties dans la peau. Les fibres C, non myélinisées, transmettent précisément la douleur de type brûlure.

Et c'est le point : lors d'une brûlure du troisième degré, ces terminaisons sont détruites avec le derme. La zone la plus profondément brûlée devient **insensible**, tandis que les brûlures superficielles, où les récepteurs subsistent, sont les plus douloureuses. Une peau entièrement consumée ne transmet plus rien.

Le verset ne parle ni de nocicepteurs ni de derme : il décrit un châtiment. Mais la logique qu'il énonce est exactement celle du corps. Pour que la douleur dure, il faut que la peau soit refaite — et il aura fallu attendre la neurophysiologie pour comprendre pourquoi.

## Les yeux qui débordent

Le Coran ne parle des larmes qu'à deux reprises. La racine *d-m-'* — celle du mot *dam'*, la larme — n'apparaît que dans deux versets de tout le livre, et les deux emploient le même verbe.

*« … tu vois leurs yeux **déborder** de larmes, à cause de la vérité qu'ils ont reconnue. »* (Coran 5:83)

*« … ils s'en retournèrent, les yeux **débordant** de larmes, de tristesse de ne pas trouver de quoi dépenser. »* (Coran 9:92)

Le verbe est *tafîdu*, de la racine *f-y-d*. Il ne signifie pas « couler » ni « verser » : il signifie **déborder**, se répandre par-dessus bord. C'est le mot qu'on emploie pour un récipient déjà plein, dont le contenu franchit les bords. Le Coran aurait pu dire que les larmes coulent ; il dit qu'elles débordent.

Or c'est exactement ce qui se produit. L'œil ne fabrique pas des larmes au moment où l'on pleure : il en produit en permanence, jour et nuit, éveillé ou endormi. La glande lacrymale sécrète un film continu qui humecte la cornée, puis s'évacue par deux minuscules orifices au coin interne de la paupière, les points lacrymaux, descend par le canal lacrymo-nasal et se déverse dans les fosses nasales. C'est un circuit fermé, qui fonctionne sans arrêt et sans qu'on s'en aperçoive.

Pleurer, ce n'est pas déclencher les larmes. C'est produire davantage que ce que ce circuit d'évacuation peut absorber. Le trop-plein franchit alors le bord de la paupière et coule sur le visage.

Le mot choisi décrit donc la chose telle qu'elle est : un débordement, et non une mise en route. Et c'est aussi ce qui explique un fait de tous les jours — pleurer fait couler le nez, parce que le canal qui évacue les larmes débouche dans les narines.

## L'allaitement et le lait

*« Nous vous abreuvons de ce qui se trouve dans leurs ventres, entre les excréments et le sang : un lait pur, facile à avaler pour les buveurs. »* (Coran 16:66)

La localisation est exacte au sens physiologique : les nutriments issus de la digestion intestinale passent dans la circulation sanguine, et c'est le sang qui apporte à la glande mammaire les éléments dont elle compose le lait. Le lait se forme donc bien à partir de ce qui transite entre le contenu intestinal et le sang.

## Ce qu'il faut retenir

Rien dans ce chapitre n'a eu besoin d'être forcé. Un texte du VIIᵉ siècle décrit la formation de l'être humain comme une succession d'états, chacun nommé par un mot que la langue arabe possédait déjà et dont le sens propre désigne exactement ce qui se produit à ce moment-là.

Et il le fait sans reprendre une seule des explications savantes de son temps — ni le sang menstruel coagulé d'Aristote, ni les humeurs de Galien. Là où la médecine grecque se trompait, le Coran se tait ; là où il parle, il tombe juste.

chapters.title: L'abeille, la mouche et les vents
chapters.text:
## L'abeille et le lieu du miel

*« Et ton Seigneur révéla aux abeilles : "Prenez des demeures dans les montagnes, les arbres et les treillages que les hommes font. Puis mangez de toute espèce de fruits et suivez les sentiers de votre Seigneur, rendus faciles pour vous." De leurs ventres sort une boisson aux couleurs variées, dans laquelle il y a une guérison pour les gens. »* (Coran 16:68-69)

Le point qui retient l'attention est simple : le verset dit que le miel **sort du ventre** de l'abeille.

Ce n'est pas ce qu'un observateur aurait spontanément supposé. On aurait plutôt imaginé que l'abeille récolte un liquide sucré et le dépose tel quel dans les alvéoles — un transport, non une transformation interne.

L'entomologie a établi le mécanisme réel. L'abeille possède un organe appelé **jabot** (ou « estomac à miel ») où le nectar est stocké pendant le vol. Cet organe fait partie de l'intestin antérieur et il est **séparé de l'estomac digestif** — le ventricule, ou intestin moyen — par une valve appelée proventricule. Cette valve ne laisse passer vers la digestion que ce qui doit l'être, et empêche les sucs digestifs de contaminer le nectar stocké.

Dans le jabot, le nectar est mêlé à des enzymes qui commencent à en transformer les sucres. L'abeille le régurgite ensuite. Le miel sort donc bien du ventre de l'abeille, au terme d'un passage interne — et non d'une simple collecte.

## Ce que mange l'abeille : un mot mal traduit

Les traductions françaises rendent presque toutes le début de 16:69 par « mangez de toute espèce de **fruits** ». Le mot arabe est *ath-thamarât* — et ce n'est pas celui qui désigne les fruits.

L'arabe coranique distingue deux termes. *Fâkiha* désigne le fruit qu'on mange pour lui-même ; le Coran l'emploie dix-huit fois, dans des contextes de nourriture et de jouissance. *Thamara* est plus large : c'est le **produit**, ce qui est engendré, le rendement — le mot sert d'ailleurs à dire le fruit d'un travail ou d'un effort.

Or l'abeille ne mange pas de fruits. Elle prélève le **nectar** au fond des corolles, le **miellat** que d'autres insectes excrètent sur les feuilles, et le **pollen**, seul aliment des larves. Rien de tout cela n'est une *fâkiha*. Tout cela, en revanche, est bien un produit végétal — une *thamara*.

Le verset ordonne donc de manger « de tout ce qui est produit », et non « de tous les fruits ». Le mot juste est employé ; c'est la traduction qui introduit l'erreur.

## « Suivez les chemins de votre Seigneur »

Le même verset contient une autre indication, plus discrète :

*« Puis mangez de toute espèce de produits, et suivez les chemins (subul) de votre Seigneur, rendus faciles pour vous. »* (Coran 16:69)

Deux ordres, dans cet ordre : butiner, puis **suivre des chemins**. Le mot *subul* est le pluriel de *sabîl*, la voie, le trajet. Il ne s'agit pas d'errance mais d'itinéraires.
